# Free vs Pro — what we charge for, and why

_Decided 2026-07-24. This is the record; if the code disagrees, the code is wrong._

The only prior written record of the commercial model is the design itself, twice
(`Fitcheck.dc.html:698`, `:797`):

> **Go Pro · £5/mo** — *"Unlimited daily looks, packing mode & cost-per-wear analytics."*

Three features. This document expands that into a full tier definition, keeps it consistent with
**Decision 4** in `CLAUDE.md` — *"the free tier must stay genuinely great — consumer apps die when the
paywall hits before the magic moment"* — and checks it against what we actually pay to serve.

---

## 1. The principle: meter what costs us money, sell what compounds

Two different things can justify a price, and confusing them is how apps end up gating their own growth.

- **Cost-to-serve.** Every AI generation costs real money. That is a *meter*, and metering it is honest.
- **Compounding value.** Analytics, planning, advice. Zero marginal cost, high willingness to pay,
  and — importantly — *worthless to a new user*. Nobody pays for cost-per-wear on day one; they pay for
  it in month three, once the data is theirs.

Everything else stays free. In particular, three things must **never** be gated:

| Never gate | Why |
|---|---|
| **The daily drop + the "why"** | It is the product. Gating it means nobody discovers the magic. |
| **The Style DNA share card** | It is a growth channel, not a feature. Charging for your own marketing is self-harm. |
| **The closet, tagging and item editing** | The closet is the moat and the switching cost. Every item added makes the product better *and* makes leaving harder. Capping it is paying to make our own retention worse. |

---

## 2. The meter: AI generations per day

**One number, easy to explain: Free gets 3 AI generations per day. Pro is unlimited.**

A "generation" is any call that spends a model request — the daily drop for an occasion, a regenerate,
or building a look around a chosen item. Reading a look that already exists is always free and always
unlimited, per Decision 5.

Three is deliberate: your predicted occasion generates automatically, leaving two for exploring another
occasion or regenerating when you dislike what you got. A user who never thinks about the limit never
hits it.

### The arithmetic, so the number is not a vibe

Haiku 4.5 at $1/1M in, $5/1M out. One text-only re-rank ≈ 1,500 in + 300 out:

```
(1500 / 1M × $1) + (300 / 1M × $5) = $0.0015 + $0.0015 ≈ $0.003 per generation
```

| Scenario | Cost/user/month |
|---|---|
| Free user, realistic ~1.5 generations/day | **≈ $0.14** |
| Free user maxing all 3 every day | **≈ $0.27** |
| Pro user, heavy — 10/day | **≈ $0.90** (vs £5 revenue) |

Item tagging is one-time and negligible: a 100-item closet is ~$0.20, ever. **Do not cap closet size.**
The saving is trivial and the damage to retention is not.

At 5% conversion, 100 users cost roughly $14–27/month to serve and return ~£25. Thin but positive — and
Pro users are cheap to serve relative to what they pay, which is the right shape. **If real usage runs
above ~2 generations/day for free users, lower the free allowance to 2 before raising the price.**

---

## 3. The tiers

### Free — the whole loop, forever

- Unlimited closet items, AI tagging, background removal, full item editing
- The daily drop: your occasion's looks with the one-sentence why
- **3 AI generations per day** (drop + regenerates + other occasions)
- Wear logging, the Fit Diary, streaks — *the habit loop is what creates a payer*
- Style DNA card and sharing
- Up to **10 saved outfits**
- Weather, location, rain guard, all preferences

### Pro — £5/mo

| # | Feature | Type | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Unlimited generations** — regenerate freely, all four occasions daily | Meter | Design (*"unlimited daily looks"*) |
| 2 | **Style an outfit with this** — build a look around any piece, unlimited | Meter | New |
| 3 | **Packing mode** — a trip in, a capsule and per-day looks out | Meter + planning | Design |
| 4 | **Cost-per-wear analytics** — the full Wear Stats screen | Compounding | Design |
| 5 | **Gap analysis** — *"a camel overcoat unlocks 14 new outfits"* | Compounding | New |
| 6 | **Unlimited saved outfits + favourites** | Compounding | New |

Items 1, 3 and 4 are the design's own three. Items 2, 5 and 6 are what turns them into a bundle worth a
recurring charge rather than a single metered button.

### Why gap analysis is the sharpest one

It is the only feature that answers *"what should I buy?"* — the highest-intent question a wardrobe app
can be asked. It is also the natural home for the design's **"See curated picks"** CTA (`:767`), which
makes it the bridge to a second revenue line. It is deliberately Pro from day one so that affiliate
revenue never becomes a reason to degrade the free experience.

### Why packing mode earns its place

It is the only Pro feature with a hard deadline attached — you need it *this week, before the flight* —
which converts far better than an open-ended benefit. It is episodic, so it does not inflate steady-state
cost, and it is the most screenshot-shareable output the product could produce.

**Packing mode does not exist in any spec, design or plan.** It needs a brainstorm before a plan; see §5.

---

## 4. What this means for the code

**Everything Pro must route through one seam.** Gating six screens by retrofitting `if (isPro)` into
each is how this becomes unmaintainable — and it is exactly the fork where this project's stated
preference is the extensible option, not the minimal diff.

`lib/outfits/quota.ts` is already that seam for generations (`assertCanGenerate` currently returns
unconditionally). It needs to widen into `lib/billing/entitlements.ts` covering both meters and
capabilities:

```ts
type Entitlements = {
  generationsPerDay: number | null;   // null = unlimited
  savedOutfits: number | null;
  analytics: boolean;                 // wear stats + cost-per-wear
  gapAnalysis: boolean;
  packingMode: boolean;
};
```

Two hard rules:

1. **"Limited" is a state, not an error.** A user at their daily limit sees an explanation and an
   upgrade path, never a thrown exception or a blank screen. This is already the stated design of the
   regenerate-quota plan; it now applies everywhere.
2. **Read entitlements server-side only.** A client-side check is a suggestion.

Until billing exists, `entitlements()` returns the free tier for everyone, with a local override so Pro
surfaces can be built and tested. **No Stripe until the features are worth paying for.**

---

## 5. Plan order, revised for this

Two new plans, and one insertion point that matters.

**`entitlements` must land before any Pro-gated feature is built.** Wear stats, gap analysis, saved
outfits and packing mode are all gated; building them first means retrofitting the gate into four
screens afterwards.

| # | Plan | Status | Tier impact |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `seasons-soft-preference` | written | — |
| 2 | `design-tokens` | written | — |
| 3 | `item-data-completeness` | written | price → cost-per-wear |
| 4 | `outfit-detail-wear-logging` | written | wear data → all analytics |
| 5 | `item-detail-rebuild` | written | ships Pro feature #2 behind the seam |
| 6 | `fit-diary` | written | free (retention) |
| 7 | **`entitlements`** | **to write** | **the seam — blocks 8, 10, 11** |
| 8 | `regenerate-quota` | **rewrite** | becomes Pro #1; 3/day free |
| 9 | `profile-hub` → `settings` | written | Pro card gets a real state |
| 10 | `wear-stats` | written — **add the gate** | Pro #4 + #5 |
| 11 | **`packing-mode`** | **needs a brainstorm first** | Pro #3 |
| 12 | `item-signals-in-generator` | written | — |
| 13 | `cutout-backfill` | written | — |
| 14 | `route-url-audit` | written | runs last |
| 15 | `generator-audit` | written | last before billing |
| 16 | *billing / Stripe* | not scoped | after 1–15 |

Note the ordering consequence: **`item-detail-rebuild` (5) ships a Pro feature before the seam exists
(7).** Either move the seam earlier, or have that plan call `assertCanGenerate` — which already exists —
and let the entitlements plan widen it underneath. **The second is cheaper and is the recommendation.**

---

## 6. Open questions

- **Annual pricing.** £5/mo implies roughly £48/yr at the usual discount. Not decided.
- **Trial.** A 7-day Pro trial after the fifth wear log would land when the analytics finally have data
  to show. Not decided.
- **Regional pricing.** GBP is the design's currency; the app targets the EU and Supabase is EU-region.
  Needs a decision alongside the currency setting in Settings.
- **"See curated picks."** Affiliate partner, disclosure requirements, and whether recommendations may
  ever influence what the stylist suggests. **They must not** — the moment purchase incentives touch
  outfit ranking, the one-sentence why stops being trustworthy, and that sentence is the product.

content.text:
Two documents and one new plan. You were right that one metered button isn't a product — here's what makes it a bundle.

**`docs/MONETISATION.md`**

The anchor is the design itself, which states the model twice and nobody had read: **£5/mo for "unlimited daily looks, packing mode & cost-per-wear analytics."** Three features. I expanded that to six:

| Pro | Type |
|---|---|
| Unlimited generations | meter *(design)* |
| Style an outfit with this | meter |
| **Packing mode** | meter + planning *(design)* |
| Cost-per-wear analytics | compounding *(design)* |
| **Gap analysis** | compounding |
| Unlimited saved outfits | compounding |

The organising principle: **meter what costs money, sell what compounds.** Analytics cost us nothing to serve but are worthless on day one and valuable in month three — that's the shape of a subscription. Generations are a real per-call cost, so metering them is honest rather than artificial.

**Gap analysis is the sharpest one.** It's the only feature that answers *"what should I buy?"* — highest-intent question a wardrobe app can be asked, and the natural home for the design's "See curated picks". **Packing mode earns its place** because it's the only Pro feature with a deadline attached — you need it *before the flight* — and deadlines convert far better than open-ended benefits.

**The number, with arithmetic rather than a vibe.** A re-rank call is ~1,500 in + 300 out on Haiku ≈ **$0.003**. So 3 free generations/day is ~$0.14/user/month realistically, ~$0.27 if maxed. At 5% conversion, 100 users cost $14–27 and return ~£25. **Thin but positive** — and I wrote the trigger down: if real usage runs above ~2/day, lower the free allowance to 2 *before* raising the price.

**Three things I refused to gate**, and I'd push back if you want to:
- The daily drop and the why — it *is* the product
- The Style DNA share card — that's a growth channel; charging for your own marketing is self-harm
- Closet size and tagging — the closet is the moat and the switching cost. Capping it saves ~$0.20/user and makes retention worse

**The ordering consequence you asked about.** The entitlements seam has to land **before** any Pro feature, or the gate gets retrofitted into four screens. So it's now #7, ahead of regenerate-quota, wear-stats and packing mode. Two plans need revision: `regenerate-quota` becomes Pro #1 (rewrite), and `wear-stats` as written **has no gate** — flagged in the README.

One wrinkle I couldn't design away: `item-detail-rebuild` (#5) ships a Pro feature before the seam exists (#7). Cheapest fix is having it call the existing `assertCanGenerate` and letting entitlements widen it underneath — noted in both docs.

**`todo/2026-07-24-entitlements.md`** is written. While drafting it I hit something worth telling you now: **the existing RLS policy lets a user update their own `profiles` row — including `tier`.** Fine today since nothing is paid, but that's "set yourself to Pro" the moment billing exists. Recorded in the migration and the PR body.

Still needs you: **packing mode has no design and no spec** — the design names it and specifies nothing. That one genuinely wants a brainstorm before I write a plan.

# Packing Mode — Scoping

_Scoped 2026-07-24. **Not a plan.** Brainstorm the open decisions before writing one._

## Question

The design sells Pro on three features (`Fitcheck.dc.html:697`): *"Unlimited daily looks, **packing
mode** & cost-per-wear analytics."* Two of those exist as plans. What is packing mode?

## Answer

Nobody has said. It appears **once**, inside a marketing sentence on a card — no screen, no data model,
no mention in `fitcheck-complete-spec.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `docs/prototype-review.md`, or any plan. It is
the only Pro feature with no specification at all.

That makes it the highest-uncertainty item in the queue and the reason this is a scoping doc rather than
a plan.

## Why it is worth building anyway

Of the six Pro features in `docs/MONETISATION.md`, packing mode is the only one with a **deadline
attached** — you need it *this week, before the flight*. Deadline-driven features convert far better
than open-ended benefits, and the urgency is recurring without being constant.

It is also episodic, so it does not inflate steady-state serving cost, and its output — a laid-out
capsule wardrobe for a trip — is the most screenshot-shareable thing the product could produce.

## The likely shape

A trip goes in, a capsule and a schedule come out:

**Input:** destination, dates, and the occasions expected (work / everyday / evening / weekend, probably
weighted — "3 work days, 2 evenings").

**Output, two parts:**
1. **The capsule** — the *minimum set of items* that can dress every day of the trip. This is the real
   product. "Take these 9 pieces" is worth more than any individual outfit.
2. **A look per day**, drawn from that capsule, matched to the destination's forecast.

## What already exists that this reuses

Genuinely a lot — this is more assembly than invention:

| Need | Already built |
|---|---|
| Destination weather | `lib/weather/` — Open-Meteo + geocoding, forecast by coordinates |
| Occasion → formality band | `lib/generator/rules.ts` (`personalBand`, `applyFormalityOverride`) |
| Building and scoring outfits | `lib/generator/` — candidates, colour, score, rank |
| Naming a look + the why | `lib/generator/rerank.ts` |
| Persisting a set of outfits | `lib/outfits/` — the daily-drop write path generalises |
| Gating it | `lib/billing/entitlements.ts` (`packingMode`) once the entitlements plan ships |

## The one genuinely new algorithm

Everything above produces outfits **one at a time and independently**. A capsule is the opposite: a
*set* problem, where the goal is maximum outfit coverage from minimum items, and the pieces must be
chosen together because they have to recombine across days.

That is set cover — NP-hard in general, trivially fine at wardrobe scale with a greedy heuristic

# Free vs Pro — what we charge for, and why

_Decided 2026-07-24. This is the record; if the code disagrees, the code is wrong._

The only prior written record of the commercial model is the design itself, twice
(`Fitcheck.dc.html:698`, `:797`):

> **Go Pro · £5/mo** — *"Unlimited daily looks, packing mode & cost-per-wear analytics."*

Three features. This document expands that into a full tier definition, keeps it consistent with
**Decision 4** in `CLAUDE.md` — *"the free tier must stay genuinely great — consumer apps die when the
paywall hits before the magic moment"* — and checks it against what we actually pay to serve.

---

## 1. The principle: meter what costs us money, sell what compounds

Two different things can justify a price, and confusing them is how apps end up gating their own growth.

- **Cost-to-serve.** Every AI generation costs real money. That is a *meter*, and metering it is honest.
- **Compounding value.** Analytics, planning, advice. Zero marginal cost, high willingness to pay,
  and — importantly — *worthless to a new user*. Nobody pays for cost-per-wear on day one; they pay for
  it in month three, once the data is theirs.

Everything else stays free. In particular, three things must **never** be gated:

| Never gate | Why |
|---|---|
| **The daily drop + the "why"** | It is the product. Gating it means nobody discovers the magic. |
| **The Style DNA share card** | It is a growth channel, not a feature. Charging for your own marketing is self-harm. |
| **The closet, tagging and item editing** | The closet is the moat and the switching cost. Every item added makes the product better *and* makes leaving harder. Capping it is paying to make our own retention worse. |

---

## 2. The meter: AI generations per day

**One number, easy to explain: Free gets 3 AI generations per day. Pro is unlimited.**

A "generation" is any call that spends a model request — the daily drop for an occasion, a regenerate,
or building a look around a chosen item. Reading a look that already exists is always free and always
unlimited, per Decision 5.

Three is deliberate: your predicted occasion generates automatically, leaving two for exploring another
occasion or regenerating when you dislike what you got. A user who never thinks about the limit never
hits it.

### The arithmetic, so the number is not a vibe

Haiku 4.5 at $1/1M in, $5/1M out. One text-only re-rank ≈ 1,500 in + 300 out:

```
(1500 / 1M × $1) + (300 / 1M × $5) = $0.0015 + $0.0015 ≈ $0.003 per generation
```

| Scenario | Cost/user/month |
|---|---|
| Free user, realistic ~1.5 generations/day | **≈ $0.14** |
| Free user maxing all 3 every day | **≈ $0.27** |
| Pro user, heavy — 10/day | **≈ $0.90** (vs £5 revenue) |

Item tagging is one-time and negligible: a 100-item closet is ~$0.20, ever. **Do not cap closet size.**
The saving is trivial and the damage to retention is not.

At 5% conversion, 100 users cost roughly $14–27/month to serve and return ~£25. Thin but positive — and
Pro users are cheap to serve relative to what they pay, which is the right shape. **If real usage runs
above ~2 generations/day for free users, lower the free allowance to 2 before raising the price.**

---

## 3. The tiers

### Free — the whole loop, forever

- Unlimited closet items, AI tagging, background removal, full item editing
- The daily drop: your occasion's looks with the one-sentence why
- **3 AI generations per day** (drop + regenerates + other occasions)
- Wear logging, the Fit Diary, streaks — *the habit loop is what creates a payer*
- Style DNA card and sharing
- Up to **10 saved outfits**
- Weather, location, rain guard, all preferences

### Pro — £5/mo

| # | Feature | Type | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Unlimited generations** — regenerate freely, all four occasions daily | Meter | Design (*"unlimited daily looks"*) |
| 2 | **Style an outfit with this** — build a look around any piece, unlimited | Meter | New |
| 3 | **Packing mode** — a trip in, a capsule and per-day looks out | Meter + planning | Design |
| 4 | **Cost-per-wear analytics** — the full Wear Stats screen | Compounding | Design |
| 5 | **Gap analysis** — *"a camel overcoat unlocks 14 new outfits"* | Compounding | New |
| 6 | **Unlimited saved outfits + favourites** | Compounding | New |

Items 1, 3 and 4 are the design's own three. Items 2, 5 and 6 are what turns them into a bundle worth a
recurring charge rather than a single metered button.

### Why gap analysis is the sharpest one

It is the only feature that answers *"what should I buy?"* — the highest-intent question a wardrobe app
can be asked. It is also the natural home for the design's **"See curated picks"** CTA (`:767`), which
makes it the bridge to a second revenue line. It is deliberately Pro from day one so that affiliate
revenue never becomes a reason to degrade the free experience.

### Why packing mode earns its place

It is the only Pro feature with a hard deadline attached — you need it *this week, before the flight* —
which converts far better than an open-ended benefit. It is episodic, so it does not inflate steady-state
cost, and it is the most screenshot-shareable output the product could produce.

---

**Everything Pro must route through one seam.** Gating six screens by retrofitting `if (isPro)` into
each is how this becomes unmaintainable — and it is exactly the fork where this project's stated
preference is the extensible option, not the minimal diff.

unconditionally). It needs to widen into `lib/billing/entitlements.ts` covering both meters and
capabilities:

```ts

  generationsPerDay: number | null;   // null = unlimited
  savedOutfits: number | null;
  analytics: boolean;                 // wear stats + cost-per-wear
  gapAnalysis: boolean;
  packingMode: boolean;
```

   upgrade path, never a thrown exception or a blank screen. This is already the stated design of the
   regenerate-quota plan; it now applies everywhere.
2. **Read entitlements server-side only.** A client-side check is a suggestion.

surfaces can be built and tested. **No Stripe until the features are worth paying for.**

---

## 5. Plan order, revised for this

Two new plans, and one insertion point that matters.

**`entitlements` must land before any Pro-gated feature is built.** Wear stats, gap analysis, saved
outfits and packing mode are all gated; building them first means retrofitting the gate into four
screens afterwards.

| 4 | `outfit-detail-wear-logging` | written | wear data → all analytics |
| 5 | `item-detail-rebuild` | written | ships Pro feature #2 behind the seam |
| 6 | `fit-diary` | written | free (retention) |

| 8 | `regenerate-quota` | **rewrite** | becomes Pro #1; 3/day free |

| 14 | `route-url-audit` | written | runs last |

| 16 | *billing / Stripe* | not scoped | after 1–15 |

(7).** Either move the seam earlier, or have that plan call `assertCanGenerate` — which already exists —
and let the entitlements plan widen it underneath. **The second is cheaper and is the recommendation.**

---

- **Annual pricing.** £5/mo implies roughly £48/yr at the usual discount. Not decided.
- **Trial.** A 7-day Pro trial after the fifth wear log would land when the analytics finally have data
  to show. Not decided.

  Needs a decision alongside the currency setting in Settings.

  ever influence what the stylist suggests. **They must not** — the moment purchase incentives touch
  outfit ranking, the one-sentence why stops being trustworthy, and that sentence is the product.

**`scoping/2026-07-24-packing-mode-scoping.md`** — same shape as the women's-wardrobe doc: what's known, what it reuses, what's genuinely new, and the decisions that must land before a plan.

The short version:

**It's mostly assembly, not invention.** Destination weather, occasion→formality bands, candidate building, scoring, look naming, persistence and the entitlement gate all already exist. What's new is *one* thing — and it's a different kind of problem from anything in `lib/generator/` today.

Everything the generator does builds outfits **one at a time, independently**. A capsule is the inverse: minimum items, maximum coverage, pieces chosen *together* because they have to recombine across days. That's set cover — trivial with a greedy heuristic at wardrobe scale, but worth naming, because a plan that assumes "run the generator five times" produces five unrelated outfits needing fifteen items. That's the opposite of packing.

Also noted: that primitive is nearly the same as the **gap analysis** in the wear-stats plan — both ask "which item unlocks the most?" Whichever ships first should expose it for the other.

The seven open decisions, of which two really matter:

1. **Is laundry modelled?** Ten days with four shirts implies re-wearing. This single answer changes capsule size dramatically.
2. **What happens when you don't own it?** If the trip needs formality the wardrobe can't reach — does it say so, or fall back? This project has already fixed "silently returns nothing" three times (`personalBand`, outerwear, seasons), so it's worth deciding up front rather than discovering it again.

One consequence I flagged in `MONETISATION.md`: the Pro card's copy — *"unlimited daily looks, packing mode & cost-per-wear analytics"* — **names packing mode**. So it can't be a Pro selling point until it exists. Either it gets built before you charge, or Pro sells on the other five and the card copy changes. Worth knowing now rather than at launch.

Queue is unchanged otherwise: 15 plans in `todo/`, entitlements at #7 ahead of the Pro features, two scoping docs parked.

# Talk to the Stylist — Scoping

_Scoped 2026-07-24. **Not a plan.** Brainstorm the open decisions before writing one._

## The request

> "A button like call AI chat to speak with AI — say your preferences today, or a really special
> occasion like a business meeting or a wedding."

## The gap it fills is real and already recorded

The generator only understands **four occasions** — `everyday · work · weekend · evening`
(`lib/generator/rules.ts`) — and Refine only adjusts **formality and colour lean**. So today there is
no way to express any of:

- *"A wedding in Tuscany, outdoor, 28°"*
- *"First client meeting, I want to look senior but not stiff"*
- *"It's cold and I can't be bothered"*

A wedding is not "evening" and a client pitch is not "work". `docs/STATE.md` already lists **"free-text
occasion intent (Plan-06 addition C)"** as unbuilt scope, and the occasion-model rework
(`personalBand`) went out of its way to establish that **occasion is context, not a dress code** — this
is the natural completion of that idea.

## The important distinction: two different products are hiding in this request

### A. Intent capture — one shot, structured

A text box, or a mic. The user types or says one thing. The model turns it into **constraints**, and the
existing pipeline does the rest.

```
"outdoor wedding in Tuscany, 28°, I'm a guest"
      ↓  one structured-output call  ↓
{ label: "Wedding guest", formality: 4, bandOverride: [3.5, 5],
  paletteLean: ["stone","navy"], avoidMaterials: ["wool"],
  requireCategories: ["Outerwear"]:false, note: "outdoor, hot" }
      ↓  the generator we already have  ↓
```

- **Cost:** one small call, ~$0.001. Roughly a third of a generation.
- **Architecture:** identical to item tagging — `output_config.format`, a Zod schema through
  `forStructuredOutput()`, validated on return. Nothing new to invent.
- **Risk:** low. The output is a constrained object; it cannot say anything unexpected to the user.
- **Delivers:** essentially all of the stated need — special occasions, daily mood, weather nuance.

### B. A conversation — multi-turn, open-ended

An actual chat. Back and forth, follow-ups, "no, not that one, something softer".

- **Cost:** unbounded. Each turn resends the history, so tokens grow quadratically with conversation
  length. This would immediately be the most expensive thing in the product — against Decision 4, which
  is not a nice-to-have but the reason the free tier can exist at all.
- **Architecture:** genuinely new. Every AI call today is one-shot and schema-constrained. A chat needs
  message persistence, streaming, turn limits, and an escape hatch when it goes off the rails.
- **Risk:** high. Open text invites off-topic use, and item names are user-controlled strings that would
  flow into the prompt — a prompt-injection surface that does not exist today.
- **Delivers:** the extra beyond A is mainly *refinement dialogue* — "warmer", "less formal", "not that
  jacket".

**Recommendation: build A first, and only consider B once A is in real use.** A is perhaps 80% of the
value for perhaps 5% of the cost and risk, and it fits the architecture we already have rather than
introducing a second one. If B is later justified, A becomes its first turn — nothing is wasted.

Notably, **B's main extra — "warmer, less formal, not that jacket" — is Refine.** The honest cheap
version of B is extending the Refine sheet with a free-text line that runs the same one-shot extractor,
not a chat transcript.

## What already exists that this reuses

| Need | Already built |
|---|---|
| Schema-constrained extraction | `lib/ai/tagging-schema.ts` — `forStructuredOutput()` strips the keywords the API rejects |
| Occasion → formality band | `lib/generator/rules.ts` — `personalBand`, `applyFormalityOverride` (already *replaces* the band, so it can dress you up past your usual ceiling) |
| Colour preference | `scoreCombo`'s lean term |
| Material exclusion by conditions | `weatherRules` |
| Cost metering | `lib/billing/entitlements.ts`, once that plan ships |
| Storing an intent per day | `occasion_overrides` (2026-07-23) is the same shape |

The occasion-model rework is what makes this cheap: because Refine's formality **replaces** the band
rather than intersecting it, a smart-casual wardrobe can already be asked for black tie. The extractor
just needs to produce that override.

## Open design decisions (brainstorm these before writing a plan)

1. **A or B?** See above. This is the decision; the rest are details.
2. **Voice or text?** "Speak with AI" may mean literal speech. Web Speech API is free and on-device in
   Safari; a hosted transcription API is not. Text-only for v1 is a defensible cut.
3. **Does an intent create a look, or replace the day?** Does "wedding on Saturday" generate a look
   *now*, or attach to Saturday so the daily drop honours it that morning? The second is much better
   product — and it is a **dated event**, which points at the Fit Diary and possibly a `events` table.
4. **What happens when the closet cannot do it?** A wedding may demand formality 5 from a wardrobe whose
   ceiling is 3. It must **say so plainly** — "nothing here reaches black tie; the closest is…". This
   project has fixed the same silent-empty failure three times (`personalBand`, outerwear, seasons);
   this feature would be the fourth if it is not designed in from the start.
5. **Free, metered, or Pro?** Option A costs about a third of a generation, so it can sit inside the
   free 3/day meter. Option B cannot — it would have to be Pro *and* turn-capped. Affects
   `docs/MONETISATION.md`.
6. **Does the extracted intent feed the learner?** `occasion_overrides` is already banking data for a
   future personalisation model. Free-text intents are far richer signal — "wedding", "first date",
   "flight" — and would be worth capturing in the same ledger from day one, even before anything reads
   them.
7. **Prompt-injection surface.** Item names, brands and subcategories are user-controlled text that
   already flow into the re-rank prompt. Adding free-text intent widens that. Nothing catastrophic is
   reachable (the model's output is schema-constrained and touches no tools), but the constraint schema
   must be the only thing that can influence generation — never raw text passed through.

## Rough scope (option A, once designed)

- `lib/ai/intent-schema.ts` — the constraint schema + its JSON-schema form
- `lib/ai/extract-intent.ts` — one Haiku call, schema-constrained, mirroring `tag-item.ts`
- `lib/generator/apply-intent.ts` — constraints → band override, lean, material exclusions
- UI: a free-text row in the Refine sheet, or a distinct entry point on the stylist screen
- Persist the intent alongside the day's looks so reopening shows *why* today looks different
- The "your closet cannot reach this" state (decision 4)

Small-to-mid — most of it is one structured call and a mapping function. **Option B is several times
larger and a different architecture.**

## Status

**Deferred by decision on 2026-07-24** — scoping only, to be discussed. Not in the execution queue.

If it were sequenced today it would sit after `item-signals-in-generator`, since both touch how
constraints reach the candidate builder, and after `entitlements` if it is metered.

# Plans

_Reorganised 2026-07-24._ Three folders, one rule: **a plan moves to `done/` only when its work is
merged to `main`** — not when the plan is written, and not when the branch is green.

| Folder | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `todo/` | Written, **not yet implemented**. Execute in the order below. |
| `done/` | Implemented and merged to `main`. Kept for history — the decisions in them are still the record of *why* the code looks the way it does. |
| `scoping/` | Not TDD plans. Research and scoping documents that need a design decision before a plan can be written. |

## Execution order (`todo/`)

Two inputs decide this order: `docs/design-review-2026-07-24.md` §8, and **`docs/MONETISATION.md`** §5 —
read that second one before executing anything from #7 onward, because it decides what is gated.

It changed twice on 2026-07-24. First when the full design review showed the "Wear this today" button is
the only wear-log write path in the product (six surfaces read what it writes, so it moved to the front).
Then again when the tiers were defined: **the entitlements seam has to exist before any Pro feature**,
or the gate gets retrofitted into four screens afterwards.

| # | Plan | Tier | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|

# Free vs Pro — what we charge for, and why

_Decided 2026-07-24. This is the record; if the code disagrees, the code is wrong._

The only prior written record of the commercial model is the design itself, twice
(`Fitcheck.dc.html:698`, `:797`):

> **Go Pro · £5/mo** — *"Unlimited daily looks, packing mode & cost-per-wear analytics."*

Three features. This document expands that into a full tier definition, keeps it consistent with
**Decision 4** in `CLAUDE.md` — *"the free tier must stay genuinely great — consumer apps die when the
paywall hits before the magic moment"* — and checks it against what we actually pay to serve.

---

## 1. The principle: meter what costs us money, sell what compounds

Two different things can justify a price, and confusing them is how apps end up gating their own growth.

- **Cost-to-serve.** Every AI generation costs real money. That is a *meter*, and metering it is honest.
- **Compounding value.** Analytics, planning, advice. Zero marginal cost, high willingness to pay,
  and — importantly — *worthless to a new user*. Nobody pays for cost-per-wear on day one; they pay for
  it in month three, once the data is theirs.

Everything else stays free. In particular, three things must **never** be gated:

| Never gate | Why |
|---|---|
| **The daily drop + the "why"** | It is the product. Gating it means nobody discovers the magic. |
| **The Style DNA share card** | It is a growth channel, not a feature. Charging for your own marketing is self-harm. |
| **The closet, tagging and item editing** | The closet is the moat and the switching cost. Every item added makes the product better *and* makes leaving harder. Capping it is paying to make our own retention worse. |

---

## 2. The meter: AI generations per day

**One number, easy to explain: Free gets 3 AI generations per day. Pro is unlimited.**

A "generation" is any call that spends a model request — the daily drop for an occasion, a regenerate,
or building a look around a chosen item. Reading a look that already exists is always free and always
unlimited, per Decision 5.

Three is deliberate: your predicted occasion generates automatically, leaving two for exploring another
occasion or regenerating when you dislike what you got. A user who never thinks about the limit never
hits it.

### The arithmetic, so the number is not a vibe

Haiku 4.5 at $1/1M in, $5/1M out. One text-only re-rank ≈ 1,500 in + 300 out:

```
(1500 / 1M × $1) + (300 / 1M × $5) = $0.0015 + $0.0015 ≈ $0.003 per generation
```

| Scenario | Cost/user/month |
|---|---|
| Free user, realistic ~1.5 generations/day | **≈ $0.14** |
| Free user maxing all 3 every day | **≈ $0.27** |
| Pro user, heavy — 10/day | **≈ $0.90** (vs £5 revenue) |

Item tagging is one-time and negligible: a 100-item closet is ~$0.20, ever. **Do not cap closet size.**
The saving is trivial and the damage to retention is not.

At 5% conversion, 100 users cost roughly $14–27/month to serve and return ~£25. Thin but positive — and
Pro users are cheap to serve relative to what they pay, which is the right shape. **If real usage runs
above ~2 generations/day for free users, lower the free allowance to 2 before raising the price.**

---

## 3. The tiers

### Free — the whole loop, forever

- Unlimited closet items, AI tagging, background removal, full item editing
- The daily drop: your occasion's looks with the one-sentence why
- **3 AI generations per day** (drop + regenerates + other occasions)
- Wear logging, the Fit Diary, streaks — *the habit loop is what creates a payer*
- Style DNA card and sharing
- Up to **10 saved outfits**
- Weather, location, rain guard, all preferences

### Pro — £5/mo

| # | Feature | Type | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Unlimited generations** — regenerate freely, all four occasions daily | Meter | Design (*"unlimited daily looks"*) |
| 2 | **Style an outfit with this** — build a look around any piece, unlimited | Meter | New |
| 3 | **Packing mode** — a trip in, a capsule and per-day looks out | Meter + planning | Design |
| 4 | **Cost-per-wear analytics** — the full Wear Stats screen | Compounding | Design |
| 5 | **Gap analysis** — *"a camel overcoat unlocks 14 new outfits"* | Compounding | New |
| 6 | **Unlimited saved outfits + favourites** | Compounding | New |

Items 1, 3 and 4 are the design's own three. Items 2, 5 and 6 are what turns them into a bundle worth a
recurring charge rather than a single metered button.

### Why gap analysis is the sharpest one

It is the only feature that answers *"what should I buy?"* — the highest-intent question a wardrobe app
can be asked. It is also the natural home for the design's **"See curated picks"** CTA (`:767`), which
makes it the bridge to a second revenue line. It is deliberately Pro from day one so that affiliate
revenue never becomes a reason to degrade the free experience.

### Why packing mode earns its place

It is the only Pro feature with a hard deadline attached — you need it *this week, before the flight* —
which converts far better than an open-ended benefit. It is episodic, so it does not inflate steady-state
cost, and it is the most screenshot-shareable output the product could produce.

**Packing mode does not exist in any spec, design or plan.** It needs a brainstorm before a plan; see §5.

---

## 4. What this means for the code

**Everything Pro must route through one seam.** Gating six screens by retrofitting `if (isPro)` into
each is how this becomes unmaintainable — and it is exactly the fork where this project's stated
preference is the extensible option, not the minimal diff.

`lib/outfits/quota.ts` is already that seam for generations (`assertCanGenerate` currently returns
unconditionally). It needs to widen into `lib/billing/entitlements.ts` covering both meters and
capabilities:

```ts
type Entitlements = {
  generationsPerDay: number | null;   // null = unlimited
  savedOutfits: number | null;
  analytics: boolean;                 // wear stats + cost-per-wear
  gapAnalysis: boolean;
  packingMode: boolean;
};
```

Two hard rules:

1. **"Limited" is a state, not an error.** A user at their daily limit sees an explanation and an
   upgrade path, never a thrown exception or a blank screen. This is already the stated design of the
   regenerate-quota plan; it now applies everywhere.
2. **Read entitlements server-side only.** A client-side check is a suggestion.

Until billing exists, `entitlements()` returns the free tier for everyone, with a local override so Pro
surfaces can be built and tested. **No Stripe until the features are worth paying for.**

---

## 5. Plan order, revised for this

Two new plans, and one insertion point that matters.

**`entitlements` must land before any Pro-gated feature is built.** Wear stats, gap analysis, saved
outfits and packing mode are all gated; building them first means retrofitting the gate into four
screens afterwards.

| # | Plan | Status | Tier impact |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `seasons-soft-preference` | written | — |
| 2 | `design-tokens` | written | — |
| 3 | `item-data-completeness` | written | price → cost-per-wear |
| 4 | `outfit-detail-wear-logging` | written | wear data → all analytics |
| 5 | `item-detail-rebuild` | written | ships Pro feature #2 behind the seam |
| 6 | `fit-diary` | written | free (retention) |
| 7 | **`entitlements`** | **to write** | **the seam — blocks 8, 10, 11** |
| 8 | `regenerate-quota` | **rewrite** | becomes Pro #1; 3/day free |
| 9 | `profile-hub` → `settings` | written | Pro card gets a real state |
| 10 | `wear-stats` | written — **add the gate** | Pro #4 + #5 |
| — | ~~`packing-mode`~~ | **deferred — scoping only** | Pro #3 in the tier above, but out of the build queue until its open decisions are discussed. See `plans/scoping/2026-07-24-packing-mode-scoping.md`. **The tier's marketing copy names it, so it cannot ship as a Pro selling point until it exists** — either build it before charging, or sell Pro on the other five. |
| 12 | `item-signals-in-generator` | written | — |
| 13 | `cutout-backfill` | written | — |
| 14 | `route-url-audit` | written | runs last |
| 15 | `generator-audit` | written | last before billing |
| 16 | *billing / Stripe* | not scoped | after 1–15 |

Note the ordering consequence: **`item-detail-rebuild` (5) ships a Pro feature before the seam exists
(7).** Either move the seam earlier, or have that plan call `assertCanGenerate` — which already exists —
and let the entitlements plan widen it underneath. **The second is cheaper and is the recommendation.**

---

## 6. Open questions

- **Annual pricing.** £5/mo implies roughly £48/yr at the usual discount. Not decided.
- **Trial.** A 7-day Pro trial after the fifth wear log would land when the analytics finally have data
  to show. Not decided.
- **Regional pricing.** GBP is the design's currency; the app targets the EU and Supabase is EU-region.
  Needs a decision alongside the currency setting in Settings.
- **"See curated picks."** Affiliate partner, disclosure requirements, and whether recommendations may
  ever influence what the stylist suggests. **They must not** — the moment purchase incentives touch
  outfit ranking, the one-sentence why stops being trustworthy, and that sentence is the product.

Scoped as `scoping/2026-07-24-stylist-chat-scoping.md`, with the queue and monetisation doc updated.

**The gap you spotted is real and already half-documented.** The generator only knows four occasions — `everyday · work · weekend · evening` — and Refine only adjusts formality and colour. A wedding isn't "evening" and a client pitch isn't "work". `docs/STATE.md` already lists *"free-text occasion intent"* as unbuilt scope, and the occasion-model rework explicitly established that **occasion is context, not a dress code**. This is the natural completion of that.

**The thing I want you to decide: there are two very different products in this request.**

**A — intent capture, one shot.** You type or say one thing; the model turns it into *constraints* and the existing pipeline does the rest:

```
"outdoor wedding in Tuscany, 28°, I'm a guest"
   → { formality: 4, band: [3.5,5], lean: ["stone","navy"], avoid: ["wool"] }
   → the generator we already have
```

Cost ≈ **$0.001**, about a third of a generation. Architecturally it's *identical to item tagging* — one `output_config.format` call through `forStructuredOutput()`. Nothing new to invent.

**B — an actual conversation.** Multi-turn, follow-ups, "no, softer". Each turn resends the history, so tokens grow **quadratically** — this would instantly become the most expensive thing in the product, against Decision 4. It also needs message persistence, streaming, turn caps, and it opens a prompt-injection surface that doesn't exist today (item names are user-controlled text already flowing into the re-rank prompt).

**I'd build A first.** Roughly 80% of the value at ~5% of the cost and risk, and it fits the architecture we have instead of adding a second one. If B is ever justified, A becomes its first turn — nothing wasted.

Worth noticing: **B's main extra — "warmer", "less formal", "not that jacket" — is Refine.** So the honest cheap version of B is a free-text line *in the Refine sheet* running the same extractor, not a chat transcript.

Two decisions in the doc I think matter most:

- **Does an intent create a look now, or claim a day?** "Wedding on Saturday" attaching to Saturday so the morning drop honours it is much better product than generating something immediately — and it makes this a *dated event*, which points at the Fit Diary.
- **What happens when the closet can't do it?** A wedding may want formality 5 from a wardrobe capped at 3. It has to say so. This project has fixed the silent-empty failure three times already (`personalBand`, outerwear, seasons); this would be the fourth if it isn't designed in from the start.

I did **not** assign it a tier — that depends entirely on A vs B, and I noted exactly that in `MONETISATION.md` rather than guessing.

# Systematic Debugging

## Overview

Random fixes waste time and create new bugs. Quick patches mask underlying issues.

**Core principle:** ALWAYS find root cause before attempting fixes. Symptom fixes are failure.

**Violating the letter of this process is violating the spirit of debugging.**

## The Iron Law

```
NO FIXES WITHOUT ROOT CAUSE INVESTIGATION FIRST
```

If you haven't completed Phase 1, you cannot propose fixes.

## When to Use

Use for ANY technical issue:
- Test failures
- Bugs in production
- Unexpected behavior
- Performance problems
- Build failures
- Integration issues

**Use this ESPECIALLY when:**
- Under time pressure (emergencies make guessing tempting)
- "Just one quick fix" seems obvious
- You've already tried multiple fixes
- Previous fix didn't work
- You don't fully understand the issue

**Don't skip when:**
- Issue seems simple (simple bugs have root causes too)
- You're in a hurry (rushing guarantees rework)
- Manager wants it fixed NOW (systematic is faster than thrashing)

## The Four Phases

You MUST complete each phase before proceeding to the next.

### Phase 1: Root Cause Investigation

**BEFORE attempting ANY fix:**

1. **Read Error Messages Carefully**
   - Don't skip past errors or warnings
   - They often contain the exact solution
   - Read stack traces completely
   - Note line numbers, file paths, error codes

2. **Reproduce Consistently**
   - Can you trigger it reliably?
   - What are the exact steps?
   - Does it happen every time?
   - If not reproducible → gather more data, don't guess

3. **Check Recent Changes**
   - What changed that could cause this?
   - Git diff, recent commits
   - New dependencies, config changes
   - Environmental differences

4. **Gather Evidence in Multi-Component Systems**

   **WHEN system has multiple components (CI → build → signing, API → service → database):**

   **BEFORE proposing fixes, add diagnostic instrumentation:**
   ```
   For EACH component boundary:
     - Log what data enters component
     - Log what data exits component
     - Verify environment/config propagation
     - Check state at each layer

   Run once to gather evidence showing WHERE it breaks
   THEN analyze evidence to identify failing component
   THEN investigate that specific component
   ```

   **Example (multi-layer system):**
   ```bash
   # Layer 1: Workflow
   echo "=== Secrets available in workflow: ==="
   echo "IDENTITY: ${IDENTITY:+SET}${IDENTITY:-UNSET}"

   # Layer 2: Build script
   echo "=== Env vars in build script: ==="
   env | grep IDENTITY || echo "IDENTITY not in environment"

   # Layer 3: Signing script
   echo "=== Keychain state: ==="
   security list-keychains
   security find-identity -v

   # Layer 4: Actual signing
   codesign --sign "$IDENTITY" --verbose=4 "$APP"
   ```

   **This reveals:** Which layer fails (secrets → workflow ✓, workflow → build ✗)

5. **Trace Data Flow**

   **WHEN error is deep in call stack:**

   See `root-cause-tracing.md` in this directory for the complete backward tracing technique.

   **Quick version:**
   - Where does bad value originate?
   - What called this with bad value?
   - Keep tracing up until you find the source
   - Fix at source, not at symptom

### Phase 2: Pattern Analysis

**Find the pattern before fixing:**

1. **Find Working Examples**
   - Locate similar working code in same codebase
   - What works that's similar to what's broken?

2. **Compare Against References**
   - If implementing pattern, read reference implementation COMPLETELY
   - Don't skim - read every line
   - Understand the pattern fully before applying

3. **Identify Differences**
   - What's different between working and broken?
   - List every difference, however small
   - Don't assume "that can't matter"

4. **Understand Dependencies**
   - What other components does this need?
   - What settings, config, environment?
   - What assumptions does it make?

### Phase 3: Hypothesis and Testing

**Scientific method:**

1. **Form Single Hypothesis**
   - State clearly: "I think X is the root cause because Y"
   - Write it down
   - Be specific, not vague

2. **Test Minimally**
   - Make the SMALLEST possible change to test hypothesis
   - One variable at a time
   - Don't fix multiple things at once

3. **Verify Before Continuing**
   - Did it work? Yes → Phase 4
   - Didn't work? Form NEW hypothesis
   - DON'T add more fixes on top

4. **When You Don't Know**
   - Say "I don't understand X"
   - Don't pretend to know
   - Ask for help
   - Research more

### Phase 4: Implementation

**Fix the root cause, not the symptom:**

1. **Create Failing Test Case**
   - Simplest possible reproduction
   - Automated test if possible
   - One-off test script if no framework
   - MUST have before fixing
   - Use the `superpowers:test-driven-development` skill for writing proper failing tests

2. **Implement Single Fix**
   - Address the root cause identified
   - ONE change at a time
   - No "while I'm here" improvements
   - No bundled refactoring

3. **Verify Fix**
   - Test passes now?
   - No other tests broken?
   - Issue actually resolved?

4. **If Fix Doesn't Work**
   - STOP
   - Count: How many fixes have you tried?
   - If < 3: Return to Phase 1, re-analyze with new information
   - **If ≥ 3: STOP and question the architecture (step 5 below)**
   - DON'T attempt Fix #4 without architectural discussion

5. **If 3+ Fixes Failed: Question Architecture**

   **Pattern indicating architectural problem:**
   - Each fix reveals new shared state/coupling/problem in different place
   - Fixes require "massive refactoring" to implement
   - Each fix creates new symptoms elsewhere

   **STOP and question fundamentals:**
   - Is this pattern fundamentally sound?
   - Are we "sticking with it through sheer inertia"?
   - Should we refactor architecture vs. continue fixing symptoms?

   **Discuss with your human partner before attempting more fixes**

   This is NOT a failed hypothesis - this is a wrong architecture.

## Red Flags - STOP and Follow Process

If you catch yourself thinking:
- "Quick fix for now, investigate later"
- "Just try changing X and see if it works"
- "Add multiple changes, run tests"
- "Skip the test, I'll manually verify"
- "It's probably X, let me fix that"
- "I don't fully understand but this might work"
- "Pattern says X but I'll adapt it differently"
- "Here are the main problems: [lists fixes without investigation]"
- Proposing solutions before tracing data flow
- **"One more fix attempt" (when already tried 2+)**
- **Each fix reveals new problem in different place**

**ALL of these mean: STOP. Return to Phase 1.**

**If 3+ fixes failed:** Question the architecture (see Phase 4.5)

## your human partner's Signals You're Doing It Wrong

**Watch for these redirections:**
- "Is that not happening?" - You assumed without verifying
- "Will it show us...?" - You should have added evidence gathering
- "Stop guessing" - You're proposing fixes without understanding
- "Ultra-think this" - Question fundamentals, not just symptoms
- "We're stuck?" (frustrated) - Your approach isn't working

**When you see these:** STOP. Return to Phase 1.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Issue is simple, don't need process" | Simple issues have root causes too. Process is fast for simple bugs. |
| "Emergency, no time for process" | Systematic debugging is FASTER than guess-and-check thrashing. |
| "Just try this first, then investigate" | First fix sets the pattern. Do it right from the start. |
| "I'll write test after confirming fix works" | Untested fixes don't stick. Test first proves it. |
| "Multiple fixes at once saves time" | Can't isolate what worked. Causes new bugs. |
| "Reference too long, I'll adapt the pattern" | Partial understanding guarantees bugs. Read it completely. |
| "I see the problem, let me fix it" | Seeing symptoms ≠ understanding root cause. |
| "One more fix attempt" (after 2+ failures) | 3+ failures = architectural problem. Question pattern, don't fix again. |

## Quick Reference

| Phase | Key Activities | Success Criteria |
|-------|---------------|------------------|
| **1. Root Cause** | Read errors, reproduce, check changes, gather evidence | Understand WHAT and WHY |
| **2. Pattern** | Find working examples, compare | Identify differences |
| **3. Hypothesis** | Form theory, test minimally | Confirmed or new hypothesis |
| **4. Implementation** | Create test, fix, verify | Bug resolved, tests pass |

## When Process Reveals "No Root Cause"

Three defects, not one. Your "still only 2 tops" was the signal that the first fix was necessary but not sufficient — thank you for pushing back.

| # | Where | What |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `candidates.ts` | Top-major loop + `slice(0, CAP)` → only 1 top of 20 ever reached ranking. **Fixed** |
| 2 | `rerank.ts:77` | Prompt said *"pick the best 3"* with **no instruction they must differ**. Model optimises one notion of "best" over a ranked list — near-duplicates are exactly what it was asked for. **Fixed** |
| 3 | `actions.ts:166` | `top[p.combo_index]?.items ?? top[0].items` — an out-of-range index silently became a **copy of the first look**. **Fixed** |

Defect 2 is almost certainly what you were seeing. Fixing coverage gave the model 20 genuinely different candidates — and it still had no reason to choose varied ones. The prompt now requires that no two looks share a top or a bottom.

Defect 3 was the sneaky one: `dedupePicks` can't catch it, because indices `25` and `30` are *different* indices that both resolved to `top[0]`. Out-of-range picks are now dropped rather than fabricated into a duplicate.

A deliberate consequence: **you may sometimes get 2 looks instead of 3.** If the model returns a repeat, you lose one look rather than seeing the same outfit twice. `saveDailyLooks` already tolerates a variable count — that's why it's delete-then-insert rather than upsert.

3. Check the three looks now use three different tops

content.text:
Yes, it can. Good question — and it exposes exactly where the guarantee stops.

What's actually enforced right now:

- **Code guarantees:** no two looks are the *same combo*. That's `dedupePicks`.
- **Prompt requests:** no two share a top, no two share a bottom. That's an *instruction to the model*, not a constraint.

Those are different things. Combo 3 (cream top + navy trousers + brown loafers) and combo 7 (cream top + stone chinos + white sneakers) are **different indices with the same top**. `dedupePicks` passes them both, because it only compares indices. An LLM instruction is a strong preference, not a guarantee — so a shared top or bottom can still get through.

**The proper fix is upstream of the model, not downstream.** Right now `rankTopN` hands over the top 20 by score, and similar-scoring combos cluster — so that list may contain the same top eight times. If instead the shortlist is diversified *before* the model sees it, then whatever three it picks are automatically distinct, and no prompt compliance is required:

```
rankTopN(20)  →  diversify  →  rerank picks 3
                    ↑
        prefer combos whose top AND bottom
        are not already in the shortlist
```

That's the "diversity pass" I declared dead earlier — and I was wrong about *where* it belongs. I tested it on the final three and concluded it wasn't needed; the right place is the shortlist. My probe couldn't see that because its combos all tied at 0.8000.

One honest limit: **a small closet can't always avoid it.** With 2 eligible tops you cannot have 3 looks with 3 different tops — something has to give. So the rule has to be *prefer* distinct and allow a repeat only when the closet forces it, which also keeps you from dropping to 2 looks unnecessarily. That's strictly better than today, where a repeat can happen even with 20 tops available.

Want me to build it? It's small — one pure function between ranking and re-ranking, plus tests. It would also make the prompt rule redundant, which is a good sign: a constraint enforced in code beats one requested in English.

content.text:
Answering your question directly, now that it's enforced rather than requested:

**Before this change: yes.** Only distinct *combos* were guaranteed. Combo 3 (cream top + navy trousers) and combo 7 (cream top + stone chinos) are different combos with the same top — both passed.

**Now: no, unless your closet forces it.** The shortlist is diversified *before* the model sees it, so no two of the 20 candidates share a top or a bottom. Whichever three it picks are distinct by construction — no prompt compliance needed.

Your question caught a second thing I'd have shipped broken. My first attempt padded the shortlist to 20, and with a 10-top / 6-bottom closet only **6** distinct combos exist — so 14 of the 20 slots would have been repeats the model was free to pick. That's the bug I was supposedly fixing, reintroduced one layer down. It now backfills only to a floor of 3.

So the honest guarantee:

- Closet supports ≥3 distinct looks → **three different tops and three different bottoms, always.**
- Closet supports fewer (e.g. 2 eligible tops) → you get a repeat, because three distinct looks don't exist. Showing 3 looks with a shared top beats showing 2. That's the only case.

Also worth knowing: the shortlist is now *shorter* on small closets — 6 real candidates instead of 6 real + 14 padded. That's intentional. Fewer, honest options beat a padded list.

Five commits on `fix/generator-coverage`. **213 tests, tsc clean, build clean** — and still unverified live, which is the check you said we'd do at the end.

One thing I'd flag for that final pass: the diversity rule keys on **tops and bottoms only**. Two looks can still share *shoes* or a *coat*. That's arguably correct — you own fewer shoes than shirts, and rotating a coat every day isn't realistic — but it's a judgment I made, not something the design specifies. Worth a look when you test.

## OPEN: Regenerate does not work properly

**Reported 2026-07-24, not yet investigated. Do not fix from this section — reproduce first.**

The exact misbehaviour was not captured, so **step one is to pin down what "not properly" means**: does
it return the *same* looks, return nothing, error, take no effect, or something else? Those have
different causes and the wrong assumption wastes the whole investigation.

### Suspects, in order of prior probability

**S1 — the pipeline is deterministic, so Regenerate legitimately returns the same looks.**

This is the strongest suspect and it is a *design* gap, not a bug. Nothing in the pipeline varies
between runs: `buildCandidates` is deterministic, `rankTopN` sorts by a pure score, and
`diversify` is greedy over that order. The model receives an identical shortlist every time. Only
Haiku's own sampling introduces variation, and it is choosing from the same 20 candidates — so the
same outfits are very likely to come back, possibly with different names.

**The mechanism to fix it already exists and is unused.** `CandidateArgs.excludeItemIds` is a real
field, threaded all the way into `isEligible` — and `app/generate/actions.ts` passes `excludeItemIds:
[]` on every call, including regenerates. Populating it with the pieces from the currently-stored looks
is the obvious implementation of "show me something else", and it needs no randomness, which keeps the
pipeline reproducible and testable.

Open question that belongs with it: should Regenerate exclude only *tops and bottoms* from the previous
set, or every piece? Excluding everything on a small closet returns nothing.

**S2 — the regenerate request is not reaching the generator as a regenerate.**
`generate({ regenerate: true })` skips the stored-look read. If the client omits or drops the flag, the
action reads today's stored set and returns it unchanged — which looks exactly like "the button does
nothing". Check the flag at the boundary before assuming anything deeper.

**S3 — the write half fails silently.** `saveDailyLooks` is delete-then-insert. If the delete succeeds
and the insert fails, the day's set is gone and the next read regenerates — or shows nothing. The
action awaits the save deliberately, so an error should surface; confirm it actually does.

**S4 — quota.** `assertCanGenerate` is a no-op today, so it cannot be the cause *yet*. It will become a
suspect the moment `2026-07-24-entitlements.md` ships, and a "limited" result rendered as an error would
look exactly like a broken button.

### First steps when this is picked up

- [ ] **Get the actual symptom from the user in their words**, or reproduce it on device and record what
      happens — not what is assumed to happen.
- [ ] Instrument the boundary: log `input.regenerate`, the combo count, the shortlist size, and the
      returned look ids on each call. One run produces evidence for S1-S3 at once.
- [ ] Compare two consecutive regenerates: identical look ids confirms S1 and kills S2/S3.
- [ ] Only then choose a fix. If it is S1, decide explicitly whether Regenerate should vary — and record
      that decision, since "deterministic" was a deliberate property of this pipeline, not an accident.

# Plans

_Reorganised 2026-07-24._ Three folders, one rule: **a plan moves to `done/` only when its work is
merged to `main`** — not when the plan is written, and not when the branch is green.

| Folder | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `todo/` | Written, **not yet implemented**. Execute in the order below. |
| `done/` | Implemented and merged to `main`. Kept for history — the decisions in them are still the record of *why* the code looks the way it does. |
| `scoping/` | Not TDD plans. Research and scoping documents that need a design decision before a plan can be written. |

## Execution order (`todo/`)

Two inputs decide this order: `docs/design-review-2026-07-24.md` §8, and **`docs/MONETISATION.md`** §5 —
read that second one before executing anything from #7 onward, because it decides what is gated.

It changed twice on 2026-07-24. First when the full design review showed the "Wear this today" button is
the only wear-log write path in the product (six surfaces read what it writes, so it moved to the front).

content.text:
Recorded in three places so it survives the session.

**`todo/2026-07-24-generator-audit.md`** now opens with a Status section — what's fixed (the four defects, with the before/after coverage table) and what's still open — then a dedicated **"OPEN: Regenerate does not work properly"** section.

I deliberately wrote it as *not root-caused*, because I haven't measured it. The first step listed is to pin down what "not properly" actually means — same looks back, nothing, an error, or no effect — since those have different causes and guessing wrong burns the whole investigation.

Four suspects recorded, with one clearly ahead:

**S1 — the pipeline is deterministic, so Regenerate honestly returns the same looks.** `buildCandidates` is deterministic, `rankTopN` is a pure sort, `diversify` is greedy over that order. The model gets an identical shortlist every time, so only its own sampling varies — same outfits, maybe different names. That's a design gap, not a bug.

And the fix mechanism **already exists and is unused**: `CandidateArgs.excludeItemIds` is a real field, threaded all the way into `isEligible`, and `actions.ts` passes `excludeItemIds: []` on *every* call including regenerates. Feeding it the pieces from the currently-stored looks is the natural implementation of "show me something else" — and it needs no randomness, which keeps the pipeline reproducible and testable.

The others: the `regenerate` flag not reaching the action (looks identical to a dead button), a half-failed delete-then-insert in `saveDailyLooks`, and quota — which *can't* be the cause today since `assertCanGenerate` is a no-op, but becomes one the moment entitlements ships.

Also updated the plans README (row 15 now says partially done, branch unmerged) and my session memory, so a future session resumes with the branch state and the open symptom rather than rediscovering it.

Branch `fix/generator-coverage` sits at 5 commits, unmerged, 213 tests / tsc / build green. Say the word when you want the PR opened, or leave it until the full generator pass.
